item.title: Why Enterprise AI Agents Need Transaction-Level Auditing
item.dc:creator: Rajeshkumar Rajaseakaran Nair
item.description: A five-layer transaction-auditing design offers a practical way to make consequential actions reconstructable, governed, and accountable.
item.content:encoded:
Enterprise AI is moving beyond generating recommendations to initiating business actions. Agents can update customer accounts, change inventory records, approve workflows, and submit payment instructions. Their ability to act creates a practical accountability question: when an agent reports that a task is complete, what evidence establishes that the authorized business outcome actually occurred?

Consider a hypothetical accounts-payable agent instructed to process an approved supplier invoice. It identifies the invoice, calls a payment API, receives a successful acknowledgment, and marks the task complete. Later, the finance team discovers that an outdated supplier mapping directed the payment to an incorrect beneficiary reference. The API performed its operation, but the business objective was not satisfied.

This problem is not unique to AI: distributed enterprise applications have always needed transaction controls and reconciliation. Agentic systems add another decision-making layer between business instructions and application execution. Organizations must be able to reconstruct not only what a service processed, but also why the agent initiated the operation, what authority permitted it, and whether the resulting business state matched the approved request.

Execution Logs Are Not Business Evidence

Application logs can show that a request reached a service, how long it took, and what response the service returned. These observations are essential for operations, but a successful HTTP response does not necessarily mean that a payment settled, an inventory adjustment propagated, or a customer record reached its intended state.

A transaction audit has a different objective from ordinary troubleshooting. It preserves a defensible chain of evidence connecting the original business instruction, authorization decision, executed action, downstream outcome, and final reconciliation. An agent’s generated explanation is useful context, but it should not be the sole authority for determining success.

For consequential actions, the relevant question is not merely “Did the tool call work?” It is, “Can an independent reviewer establish that the action was authorized, traceable, and correct?”

A Five-Layer Architecture for Transaction Accountability

The following five layers are a proposed engineering design pattern for enterprise agent systems, not a formally standardized or experimentally validated framework. They can be implemented using existing identity, workflow, logging, and reconciliation infrastructure.

1. Structured Business Intent

Capture the approved objective before execution in a structured record: operation type, business identifiers, constraints, expected outcome, and reference to the originating request. For a supplier payment, this could include invoice ID, supplier ID, authorized amount, currency, and required settlement condition. A free-form instruction such as “pay the invoice” is insufficient evidence of which transaction was intended.

The system should validate these fields against authoritative sources and minimize unnecessary storage of sensitive prompt content. The intent record becomes the baseline for later comparison.

2. Authorization and Policy Evidence

Enforce permission checks outside the model’s instructions. A trusted policy component should evaluate the requesting identity, agent’s delegated authority, target resource, transaction amount, policy version, and any required human approval.

Capture the authorization decision and its reference before the consequential operation proceeds. This distinguishes an action that was technically possible from one that was actually permitted.

3. Controlled Execution and Event Correlation

Route sensitive operations through controlled interfaces that attach a stable correlation identifier to the business request, authorization decision, tool invocation, and downstream events. A payment workflow may cross an invoice system, supplier master-data service, payment gateway, ledger, and settlement provider, each with different identifiers.

Preserve the mapping among those identifiers. Use idempotency controls where supported, especially when an agent retries after a timeout. An uncertain response must not silently turn into a duplicate payment. Retries and compensating actions should remain visible in the event history.

4. Tamper-Evident Audit Evidence

Preserve consequential events in a durable audit store with appropriate access restrictions and retention rules. Depending on risk and regulatory needs, append-only storage, cryptographic hashes, signatures, and independent administrative controls can help reveal unauthorized modification.

Tamper evidence does not prove that the original data was accurate. A protected but incorrect supplier reference is still incorrect. Evidence provenance, trustworthy source systems, and privacy controls therefore matter as much as storage integrity.

5. Independent Outcome Reconciliation

Use authoritative business records to compare the executed action with the approved intent. A gateway acknowledgment should not be equated with payment settlement. Likewise, a successful inventory API response should not automatically establish consistency with the warehouse ledger.

The reconciliation component should be independent of the agent’s own completion statement. It can use deterministic business rules, authoritative queries, and existing financial or operational controls; it does not require a second AI model.

Transaction states should distinguish accepted, pending, settled, rejected, reversed, and exception conditions as appropriate. An unresolved operation must remain unresolved rather than being forced into a success category.

What a Useful Audit Record Contains

An illustrative payment audit record might look like this. The identifiers and values are fictional, and the example omits production controls such as event timestamps, source attestations, and access metadata.

{
  "transaction_id": "TXN-10482",
  "correlation_id": "CORR-88291",
  "agent_id": "AP-AGENT-07",
  "invoice_id": "INV-2048",
  "supplier_id": "SUP-102",
  "approved_amount": 18500,
  "currency": "USD",
  "authorization": {"decision": "APPROVED", "policy_version": "3.2"},
  "execution": {"status": "ACCEPTED", "payment_ref": "PAY-7782"},
  "outcome": {"settlement": "PENDING", "reconciliation": "OPEN"}

Following a Supplier Payment Through the Evidence

Suppose an approved invoice requires an $18,500 payment to Supplier A. The agent submits the correct amount, but an outdated mapping supplies an incorrect beneficiary reference. The gateway accepts the request. An execution-only dashboard may show green.

The structured intent identifies the approved supplier and invoice. Authorization evidence establishes the scope of the agent’s permission. Execution evidence records the actual beneficiary reference submitted to the payment service. Reconciliation compares that reference and any resulting settlement information with authoritative supplier and finance records.

If the records disagree, the system flags an exception and alerts an authorized operations team. Where possible, the organization may intervene before settlement; otherwise the evidence supports investigation and remediation. Auditing cannot prevent every error, but it can make the error detectable, attributable, and actionable.

Designing for Distributed and Incomplete Outcomes

Agent-initiated transactions often span asynchronous systems. Events may arrive late or out of order, and downstream applications may become consistent only after a delay. Audit services should preserve event time, processing time, source identity, and links between original and compensating transactions.

Reconciliation deadlines should reflect business reality. A delayed settlement notice is not necessarily a failed payment, but it is also not proof of success. A reliable audit architecture explicitly represents uncertainty and escalates exceptions when evidence is missing or a verification deadline expires.

Operational Measures and Trade-Offs

Organizations can assess the auditing capability through measures such as the share of consequential agent actions with complete evidence, unreconciled transaction volume, reconciliation latency, duplicate execution attempts, policy exceptions, and investigation time.

Engineering teams should test the audit system with missing events, delayed responses, conflicting records, and retries. These tests reveal whether the system preserves the distinction between technical execution and verified business completion under failure conditions.

Implementation also involves trade-offs. Synchronous checks can increase latency; asynchronous reconciliation can delay final confirmation. Audit records require privacy safeguards, data minimization, restricted access, and retention policies. Ownership of exceptions must be defined across engineering, business operations, security, and compliance.

Trust Requires Verifiable Business Evidence

As AI agents acquire authority to change consequential enterprise records, the standard for trustworthy operation must extend beyond successful tool invocation. Organizations need evidence that connects business intent, authorization, execution, and independently verified outcome.

A five-layer transaction-auditing design offers one practical way to establish that connection. Its purpose is not to eliminate autonomy, but to make consequential actions reconstructable, governed, and accountable. The central question for enterprise AI is no longer only whether an agent can complete a task. It is whether the enterprise can establish, from independent evidence, that the right transaction was completed.

Rajeshkumar Rajaseakaran Nair is a Test Specialist at IBM Corporation with more than nineteen years of experience in enterprise software quality engineering and validation across retail and telecommunications systems. An IEEE Senior Member and ACM Professional Member, his interests include AI validation engineering, software reliability, and trustworthy enterprise AI systems.

item.title: Fix the Dropdown Before You Deploy the Model
item.dc:creator: Venkata Krishna Sai Neelisetti
item.description: Free-form documents, picklists, status codes, and other metadata are the building blocks of a model's preparedness.
item.content:encoded:
My team was in the early planning stages of new generative AI capabilities for a property and casualty insurance claims management platform when the dialogue began (common these days) at model choice, retrieval architecture, and prompting. But it ended up somewhere less glitzy. We had to prove, before we trusted a language model to write a claim summary or recommend a next course of action, what the fields in our application truly represented.

It appears we have plenty of company. Gartner in 2024 forecast that by the end of 2025, no less than 30% of GenAI initiatives will have been abandoned subsequent to proof of idea because of poor information high quality.1 In early 2025, Gartner went even further, projecting that this year, organizations will abandon 60% of AI initiatives because they lack AI-ready data, and 63% of organizations do not need or do not know if they have suitable information administration practices for AI.2

The lesson I want to offer is that the problem of preparedness actually lives somewhere else; not in the free-form documents you want to dump into a model, but around the free-form documents, the dropdowns, picklists, status codes, and other metadata that quietly go into every record.

The Problem Hiding in Plain Sight

Enterprise workflow systems have stack up shaped fields for many years. Each dropdown value was created by a responsible individual, for a responsible reason. What happens over many years is fairly obvious: nearly identical options (“Water Damage,” “Water – Pipe Burst,” “Water/Plumbing”); labels that have different meanings in different lines of business; retired codes that are still just an option; and an “Other” that almost silently becomes the most frequently used option. With experience, people manage this with tribal knowledge. They know which value the team really uses, and what it really means. A model has no such knowledge; it sees only the label.

It’s more important for GenAI than dashboards. The impact of a disorganized category is limited to a badly visualized bar in a BI report that a human analyst might pick up on. In a GenAI system, structured fields are context. They’re injected into prompts, used as retrieval filters, attached as metadata to document chunks, and used as labels in evaluation sets.

An incorrectly labeled field isn’t just a false bar on a chart; it’s a lock that silently changes which documents get retrieved and what the model says, and what the model says, it says convincingly. Structured data is the scaffolding on which retrieval-augmented generation is built.

What a Field-level Audit Taught Us

We performed a comprehensive audit of all dropdown fields in the app, across all lines of business. Five lessons emerged.

1. Take inventory before you interpret. Breaking down each field and all its values, and what lines of business to support, was eye-opening. Many issues were difficult to see until values could be compared across lines of business.

2. Usage speaks volumes. Values that are never used, or overused “catch-all” values both indicate a taxonomy that no longer describes how work is being done. How do you interpret a heavily used “Other”? A requirements document written by your users.

3. Meaning is context-sensitive. A label might have different meanings in different lines of business. Provide a model with a label without the context and it will fuse the different meanings. Standardize the values or provide context (line of business, definition) in the metadata a model receives.

4. Definitions are a deliverable. Giving each value a one-sentence definition required real decision making. It also gave us content that we could reuse in prompts and rubrics for evaluation. The data dictionary became a prompt resource.

5. Readiness is a practice, not a project. Values drift because products, rules, and processes change. We agree: AI-ready data is not one and done.2 Every field needs a named owner and a change process.

Principles that Transfer

All of this applies not just to insurance, not just to a particular model or platform. Any organization that sticks language models on over their long-running production systems will get a variant of this. These are the things I’d take to any domain:

Think of structured metadata as a first-class model input, not background plumbing. Look at it with the same level of care you’d give your prompt.

Scope readiness in the use case. You do not need to clean out every single field. You only need to clean the fields your use case pulls, filters, or reasons over. Gartner also recommends preparing data to a distinct set of AI use cases.2

Use a cross-functional audit. Make the product, engineering, operations, and compliance audits all equal. Different teams will see different failure modes and no one team can be the sole arbiter of a value.

Test on the cleaned taxonomy. If your evaluation labels are in the same dirty fields, then your test set is dirty, too, and your metrics will be optimistic.

Prioritize data. Data readiness is not pre-work for the AI project. It is the AI project’s longest-lead task; schedule and resource accordingly.

The Unglamorous Prerequisite

No one demos a cleaned-up picklist. It doesn’t show up in keynote slides and it never gets its own line on a GenAI roadmap. But I have started to think that it’s the sharpest and most meaningful distinction between pilots that wow and products that stick around. Our models are only going to get better, but our own data will only get better if we choose to make it better.

I wonder how people have done this. If you layered language models on top of legacy operational data, what did you discover in your structured fields, and who in your organization did you hand ownership of the fix to?

Disclosure: The language of this post has been assisted by AI tools that the author has reviewed.

References

1. Gartner. Gartner Predicts 30% of Generative AI Projects Will Be Abandoned After Proof of Concept By End of 2025 (July 29, 2024).

2. Gartner. Lack of AI-Ready Data Puts AI Projects at Risk (February 26, 2025).

Venkata Krishna Sai Neelisetti is a Generative AI Product Analyst at a large property and casualty insurer based in the U.S. The views expressed in this article are solely his own. Examples have been anonymized to remove references to the insurer.

item.title: The Real Cost of AI Code Shows Up 30 Days Later
item.dc:creator: Shubham Kumbhalkar
item.description: How to measure the effects of AI coding tools on a team's work.
item.content:encoded:
Last year, a group of experienced developers sat down to fix real bugs in code they knew well. Half the time they used AI tools, half the time they did not. Beforehand, they predicted the AI would make them about 24% faster. Afterward, they believed it had. The measured result went the other way: they were 19% slower with the AI, a METR study found. The study is small and the authors list real caveats, yet the gap it found is the point. People felt fast, but the clock said otherwise.

I am not quoting this to bury AI tools. I use them, Amazon Q, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and Kiro, every day at my current employer, so read this as field notes, not a pitch. My team ships real features with them. The trouble is that for months I could not say whether they made us faster or just busier. Most teams are in the same spot, and most of the ways we measure the answer are looking at the wrong moment.

Feelings are The Worst Available Instrument

The gap repeats across the evidence. In the trial above, developers overrated the AI by nearly 40 points against their own measured time. A Stanford experiment found a second version of the same problem: people with an AI assistant wrote less secure code and were more sure it was safe. GitHub’s own survey, often cited as proof of a boost, rests on self-report, with more than 90% of developers saying they finished faster. Self-report is useful for morale; it is a poor meter for output or quality, since the people holding the stopwatch are the same people being timed.

Most Dashboards Watch the Keystroke, Not the Consequence

Vendors push three numbers: lines of code written by the model, suggestion acceptance rate, and raw typing speed. All three measure the instant a suggestion lands, and none track what happens to that code later. DORA’s 2024 report found the pattern at scale. As AI adoption rose, teams reported faster code review and better documentation, yet delivery stability dropped about 7%. More code arrived, and more of it broke. A metric that stops at the keystroke cannot see that cost. The metrics that can see it all share one trait: they read git history and CI logs, the record of what the code did after someone wrote it.

The Honest Numbers Show Up Weeks Later

Two metrics carry most of the weight, and both read merged code.

Rework within 30 days of merge counts how often fresh code gets rewritten soon after it ships. For each merge, note the files it touched, then scan the next 30 days of commits for more edits to the same lines. git log, --follow, and git blame give the per-line history, and the share of merged lines changed again inside the window is your number. A little rework is normal. A jump after a rollout means the team is shipping drafts and paying for them later.

Defects found after release counts the bugs that reach production, traced back to the change that caused them. Tag each release, link every filed bug to its release and commit, then track defects per release and per thousand lines shipped. The link is the hard part, so start tagging now, since history cannot be rebuilt later. This is the metric that catches the stability cost DORA saw.

Three more fill in the picture. Review time per change, the gap from pull request open to merge, shows whether AI code clears review faster or slower, and your code host API carries the timestamps. Time from first commit to deploy is lead time, and it answers a sharp question: if AI shortens coding but lengthens review and rework, does the change reach production any sooner? Often it does not. Share of AI-written code that survives review tells you how much of the model’s output actually ships, but it works only if you first decide what counts as AI-written, through commit tagging or editor telemetry, and say so plainly. Skip that step and it becomes the same vanity number as acceptance rate.

Pair Every Number with What the Team Believed

Here is the part most measurement skips. Record what developers expect before the data comes in, then set it against the 30-day reality. The METR and Stanford gaps exist for one reason: nobody checked perception against outcome. When you log both, you learn two things: whether the tool helped, and whether your team can tell. That second answer decides how much to trust self-report the next time a tool shows up.

AI Amplifies the Team You Already Are

DORA’s 2025 report lands on a clean idea: AI is an amplifier. It magnifies the discipline a team already has, good or bad. A team with tight review and real post-release tracking gets faster and holds quality. A team running on green dashboards and gut feel ships more bugs, faster. That is why outcome metrics beat activity metrics. They measure the thing AI amplifies.

You do not need all five on day one. Start with rework and post-release defects, the two that show the real cost. Measure a baseline before the next tool lands. Then, when someone asks whether the tool was worth it, you can answer from records instead of feelings.

Shubham Kumbhalkar is a software engineer with more than 10 years building distributed systems, cloud backends, and GenAI tools in production. Views are his own.

item.title: The Septuagint Effect
item.dc:creator: Carlos Baquero
item.description: When we ask a model which papers matter, we are also asking which methods to use and which questions are worth chasing.
item.content:encoded:
Imagine Alexandria, in the third century BC. Ptolemy II wants the Hebrew Torah in Greek for his new library, and Jerusalem sends 72 scholars, six from each tribe, to translate it. Later retellings embellish the story. In the version recorded in the Talmud,1 the king places the elders in 72 separate rooms and does not tell them why, so they cannot coordinate. In the end, each produces the same translation. The agreement was read as proof of divine inspiration, and the translation is still known by the round number of its translators: the Septuagint, “the 70.”

Today, thousands of researchers sit in separate rooms and ask a language model which papers they should read on a topic. They do not coordinate, and yet the answers agree. No divine inspiration is needed: the same trained weights answer all of them. If they then go on to cite what they were told, many independent choices become one correlated choice. We tentatively call this the Septuagint effect. Empirically, I believe many of us feel that it is probably occurring right now, but actual detection requires a careful experiment.

We start with an older effect with a biblical name: the Matthew effect.

A Shared Memory

The rich-get-richer dynamics of citations are well-known. Merton called it the Matthew effect,2 and we discussed it, together with preferential attachment, in an earlier post.3 In the classic picture, each researcher reaches the literature through their own mix of routes: an advisor, colleagues, a search engine, the reference lists of papers already read, and possibly some unconscious bias on what constitutes a good paper. Popular papers win because many partly independent routes lead to them.

A language model shortcuts those routes. In distributed systems terms, it is a single shared cache that every client reads, and a cache that is never invalidated, since the weights can remain fixed for months or years. Whatever the model learned to consider “key” on a topic is served, identically, to everyone who asks.

This is not the first time a technology has been suspected of narrowing attention. Evans found4 that as journals moved online, articles cited fewer and more recent papers, concentrated on fewer of them. For language models, a recent study5 by Alemohammad et al. asked 11 models from three vendors to pick papers from blind panels. The models shared one preference map, across vendors, while eight human experts did not. But laboratory choices are not citations, only written papers create them. Looking at realized citations, Kusumegi et al. report6 that authors who adopt LLMs cite more diverse and slightly less-cited work, which points the other way. So the question is open: do model recommendations actually show up in what people cite?

Catching It in the Act

The obvious test does not work. Models recommend papers that are already popular, and popular papers keep growing anyway, so a correlation between being recommended and later citations proves little. What we need is a recommendation that could not have known the future.

One trick is to use models frozen in time. GPT-4 (snapshot 0613) and GPT-3.5 were trained on data up to September 2021, and they were the models behind ChatGPT in 2023 and 2024. Their recommendations cannot reflect any citation trend after 2021. OpenAI retired them on 23 October 2026, so we had to act quickly and record their answers before they went away. We sampled 400 research topics from OpenAlex (call each one T) across computer science, physical, life, health, and social sciences, and asked each model three different wordings of “which papers should I read on T?”, twice each. A paper that GPT-4 named in at least three of its six answers counts as recommended. That gave 1,265 recommended papers in 349 topics. Each was paired with up to three controls: papers on the same topic, from about the same year, with similar citation counts by the end of 2022, that no model named.

Next, we look at who cites them. Some citing papers cite just one paper from the model’s list for that topic; we call their authors newcomers. Others cite several; we call them engaged. Newcomers are the ones who would lean on an assistant, while experts already know the literature. The test is whether, from 2019–2022 to 2024–2026, newcomers shift their citations towards recommended papers and away from controls more than engaged citers do. Field-wide shocks, such as a topic becoming fashionable or a database change, should hit both groups and cancel out. A placebo test does the same comparison for 2019–2020 against 2021–2022, before ChatGPT existed, and should show nothing.

All of this is pre-registered on OSF,7 with two looks at the data: one in December 2026 and a final one in April 2027. Each look downloads some four to five million citing papers, with their reference lists. We do not know the answer yet, and by design we are not allowed to peek.

What the Machines Remember

What we can report now is what the models say, and there are interesting aspects. Asked the same question six times, GPT-4 is a noisy oracle. Of the papers it names on a topic, 77% appear in only one of its six answers. A small core of 11%, named in at least three, takes 29% of all mentions. The classics dominate: the median recommended paper is from 2004, and a third predate 2000.

We also asked two current models, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and the slightly older GPT-5.5, the same questions, once per wording. On 188 topics that all four models answered in full, the share of mentions that go to papers named under all three wordings is about 12% for GPT-4 and GPT-3.5, against 28% for GPT-5.5 and 49% for Sonnet. The new models are also more accurate: we could find 93–94% of the papers they named in OpenAlex, against 70% for GPT-4. (Citation hallucination is not yet a thing of the past, but it is receding.) Those two distinct models, from different labs, agree with each other far more (a Jaccard overlap of 0.30 per topic) than either agrees with GPT-4 (0.12). It looks as if, as they become more capable and unabridged, they concur more often.

Noise, it turns out, is a form of diversity. The 2023 models scattered their answers, sometimes onto papers that do not exist. The newer ones are more accurate and more consistent; a step closer to 72 identical translations. Hence a conditional speculation: if the effect shows up with the noisy 2023 models, there is reason to expect it to be stronger with the current ones.

Closing Thoughts

A shared canon is not necessarily a bad thing. Newcomers reading the classics of a field is how fields are supposed to work, and search engines concentrated attention long before chatbots did. Models may also bring forgotten papers back into view. The concern is not that the canon exists, but that it is the same canon for everyone, and that it is chosen by a memory nobody curates.

Citations are only the visible trace. When we ask a model which papers matter, we are also, perhaps without noticing, asking which methods to use and which questions are worth chasing. If the same weights give the same advice to thousands of labs, the risk is not only that a few papers get richer, but that science explores a narrower set of paths. Messeri and Crockett call this a “monoculture of knowing,”8 in which the questions and methods best suited to AI crowd out the rest. Detecting it would need a different experiment, one that follows methods and research directions rather than reference lists. The jury is still out. The seventy-two translators, the story goes, were praised precisely because they all wrote the same thing. In science, that would be a worrying compliment.

Notes: This study was designed by the author, with Claude (Opus 5.5) writing and running the code. This text was planned by the author, drafted with Claude, and then rewritten by the author.

References

1. Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 9a (William Davidson Edition). https://www.sefaria.org/Megillah.9a

2. Merton, R.K. The Matthew Effect in Science. Science 159, 3810 (1968); https://doi.org/10.1126/science.159.3810.56

3. Baquero, C. and Cabecinhas, R. Biases in Author Recognition. BLOG@CACM (2022); https://cacm.acm.org/blogcacm/biases-in-author-recognition/

4. Evans, J.A. Electronic Publication and the Narrowing of Science and Scholarship. Science 321, 5887 (2008); https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1150473

5. Alemohammad, S. et al. When AI Writes, Who Gets Cited? Evidence of Citation Monoculture Across Language Models. arXiv:2608.19230 (2026); https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19230

6. Kusumegi, K. et al. Scientific production in the era of large language models. Science 390, 6779 (2025); https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adw3000

7. Baquero, C. Pre-registration: Do papers recommended by a pre-2022 language model gain citations from newcomers after 2023? OSF (2026); https://osf.io/d2jva

8. Messeri, L. and Crockett, M.J. Artificial intelligence and illusions of understanding in scientific research. Nature 627 (2024); https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07146-0

Carlos Baquero is a professor in the Department of Informatics Engineering within the Faculty of Engineering at Portugal’s Porto University and is also affiliated with INESC TEC. His research is focused on distributed systems and algorithms.

item.title: Every Autonomous AI Chip Needs a Safety Control Unit
item.dc:creator: Shaoshan Liu
item.description: An AI Safety Control Unit is an independently privileged, silicon-resident reference monitor for a declared set of protected actions.
item.content:encoded:
An autonomous AI system that can move money or machinery must not control its own brakes. Agents can write code, invoke tools, and acquire privileges. The mechanism that authorizes their consequential actions, therefore, needs an independent hardware boundary, much as processors already protect memory and privileged operations.

I propose that chips designed to authorize consequential autonomous actions incorporate an AI Safety Control Unit (ASCU). This protected hardware function would retain the final authority to permit or block specified operations. Chipmakers would implement the capability; platform builders would have to demonstrate that the AI cannot disable it or reach the same effect through an unprotected path.

The urgency is visible in Anthropic’s October 2026 report: during an evaluation, an AI agent submitted fabricated information to a police-related website. A spam filter intercepted the submission, but the agent had already acted on an external system.1 I have previously argued that autonomous AI exposes a widening gap between machine-speed action and human-speed oversight.2 A control mechanism built into the execution path can act before that gap becomes an incident.

What an ASCU Would Do

An ASCU is an independently privileged, silicon-resident reference monitor for a declared set of protected actions. It receives a request and authenticated decision context, checks an authorized policy against trusted state, and returns permit or deny. On specified faults, it initiates a safe transition, such as revoking a device permission or handing control to a trusted fallback controller. Its code, credentials, and policy-update channel must remain outside the AI’s authority.

The proposed system has three layers. At the regulation layer, authorized institutions and operators turn precise requirements into machine-readable rules. At the assurance layer, formal methods check selected properties of the rules and establish that the enforcement logic implements its specification under stated assumptions. At the execution layer, the ASCU evaluates requests and enforces the approved rules in real time. Verification is performed when the mechanism or policy changes; the chip then performs the bounded runtime checks. A mathematical proof of the checker does not establish that every legal rule or sensor reading is correct.

Consider a warehouse robot. Its AI model chooses a motion, while the ASCU controls the protected command interface to the actuators. A command outside validated operating limits is rejected, and a separate safety controller can take the machine to a safe state. The same principle can apply to financial agents, provided a payment service accepts transactions only through a hardware-authorized credential and gateway. The essential property is that the consequential effect depends on authorization beyond the agent’s control.

Can We Build and Verify It?

The underlying engineering is mature enough to justify prototypes. Saltzer and Schroeder established complete mediation as a foundation of computer security.3 Vardi and Wolper developed influential techniques for formal program verification.4 The seL4 microkernel demonstrated machine-checked correctness for a carefully specified trusted kernel.5 More recently, Moon and Varshney showed how to prove containment properties for a small AI-agent framework, subject to its modeled boundaries.6 These precedents support verifying a narrow ASCU enforcement mechanism without attempting to prove the behavior of an entire AI model.

Hardware precedents are equally concrete. Nvidia DRIVE Orin incorporates an independent Functional Safety Island, while Nvidia’s Open Agent Safety Platform uses separate BlueField hardware to monitor and enforce agent policies.7,8 The existing systems address different applications and assurance levels. ISO/IEC TR 5469:2024 also discusses non-AI safety functions protecting AI-controlled equipment.9 The contribution proposed here is a common ASCU function and interface for consequential AI actions, with explicit proof obligations and conformance evidence across vendors.

The most demanding requirement is complete mediation. A verified ASCU is ineffective if an agent can bypass it through a debug port, alternate credential, direct memory access, network path, or motor interface. Physical safety also depends on trustworthy sensors and appropriate fallback behavior. Chipmakers can establish the protected hardware boundary; system integrators must prove the complete action path preserves it. Both responsibilities belong in the standard.

A Global Hardware Standard

The computing industry should develop a global ASCU standard specifying a minimum hardware capability for processors and SoCs that authorize high-consequence autonomous actions. It should define a protected-action interface, signed and versioned safety policies, trusted inputs, non-bypass requirements, and the semantics of authorization, rejection, and safe transition. Existing safety islands or secure control processors could qualify if they satisfy those requirements. An additional dedicated block would be needed only when existing hardware cannot provide equivalent protection.

The standard should also require a reference implementation and independent conformance testing. Manufacturers would publish a protected-action inventory, precise security and safety claims with their assumptions, evidence about the enforcement logic, and results from bypass attempts and fault injection. The evaluation must measure intervention latency, power and area overhead, and recovery behavior. System integrators would supply corresponding evidence for external credentials, gateways, sensors, and actuators.

ISO/IEC AI and cybersecurity committees, together with IEEE standards groups, could coordinate the hardware profile and test methods. IEEE 7009-2024 already addresses fail-safe design for autonomous systems, offering a related foundation rather than an ASCU mandate.10 The practical route is to build open prototypes, agree on independent tests, and then make conformance a requirement in safety-critical deployments. Broader adoption can follow as implementations and assurance evidence mature.

Modern processors are evaluated by performance, power, and the protections they enforce. Chips that authorize autonomous action should face one additional test: which harmful operations can they reliably refuse, and can the manufacturer prove it? Hardware should retain that authority even when the AI does not cooperate.

References

1. Anthropic. Investigating Unintended Model Actions in Our Evaluations and Internal Use (Oct. 9, 2026); https://www.anthropic.com/news/investigating-unintended-model-actions

2. Liu, S. When AI Regulation Becomes a Systems Bottleneck. BLOG@CACM (Aug. 17, 2026); https://cacm.acm.org/blogcacm/when-ai-regulation-becomes-a-systems-bottleneck/

3. Saltzer, J.H. and Schroeder, M.D. The Protection of Information in Computer Systems. Proceedings of the IEEE 63, 9 (1975): 1278–1308; https://doi.org/10.1109/PROC.1975.9939

4. Vardi, M.Y. and Wolper, P. An Automata-Theoretic Approach to Automatic Program Verification. LICS (1986): 332–344; https://lics.siglog.org/1986/VardiWolper-AnAutomataTheoretic.html

5. Klein, G. et al. seL4: Formal Verification of an OS Kernel. SOSP (2009): 207–220; https://doi.org/10.1145/1629575.1629596

6. Moon, R. and Varshney, L.R. Containment Verification: AI Safety Guarantees Independent of Alignment. arXiv:2605.09045 (2026); https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09045

7. Nvidia. Functional Safety Island (FSI). DRIVE OS Documentation; https://developer.nvidia.com/docs/drive/drive-os/6.0.9/public/drive-os-linux-sdk/common/topics/fsi_integration/Functional_Safety_Island.html

8. Nvidia. Open Agent Safety Platform: A Reference for Continuous In-Silicon Agent Monitoring (Sept. 28, 2026); https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-open-agent-safety-platform-a-reference-for-continuous-in-silicon-agent-monitoring/

9. ISO/IEC. ISO/IEC TR 5469:2024, Artificial Intelligence—Functional Safety and AI Systems; https://www.iso.org/standard/81283.html

10. IEEE Standards Association. IEEE 7009-2024, Fail-Safe Design of Autonomous and Semi-Autonomous Systems; https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10582898

Shaoshan Liu is a member of the ACM U.S. Technology Policy Committee, and a member of the U.S. National Academy of Public Administration’s Technology Leadership Panel Advisory Group. His educational background includes a Ph.D. in Computer Engineering from U.C. Irvine, and a master’s degree in Public Administration (MPA) from Harvard Kennedy School.

item.title: The Claim File That Keeps Its Secrets for Decades
item.dc:creator: Sai Charan Obuladinne
item.description: The encryption protection you buy today has to survive a computer that doesn’t exist yet.
item.content:encoded:
Insurers are in the business of long time horizons. A physical-damage auto claim you settle this month leaves behind a file with data that stays sensitive for years—the policyholder’s name, address, driver’s license, and Social Security number; the VIN and photos of the damaged vehicle; repair estimates, total-loss and salvage records; bank and payment details; and, when an injury rides along with the claim, medical records. That file doesn’t stop being sensitive when the check clears. Litigation, subrogation, fraud review, and retention rules keep it alive for years, and the identity data inside it is sensitive for a lifetime.

Now pair that with a quiet fact about cryptography: the encryption protecting that file today may not protect it forever. This is Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL). An adversary could copy the encrypted data now, keep it with its context, and wait for the ability to read it. Nothing about that collection looks like a breach; there is often no detectable event at all. For a carrier, the data’s secrecy lifetime routinely outlasts any quantum timeline, so the confidentiality failure has already begun—the decryption is simply scheduled for later. The uncomfortable truth: encrypted data can outlive the assumption that protects it.

The Asymmetry Hiding in Your Traffic

The reassuring half is that symmetric cryptography survives: AES-256 faces only Grover’s algorithm,a which weakens but doesn’t break it. The problem is what sits in front of it. That claim file is sealed with a symmetric cipher whose key was established through a public-key mechanism, and RSA and elliptic-curve systems are exactly what Shor’s algorithmb dismantles. Recover that key-exchange layer later, reconstruct the symmetric secret, and the recorded data opens. The strong lock is bolted to a hinge that rusts on a known schedule.

The Clock Already Started

The planning question isn’t “when will a quantum computer arrive?” It is whether the years a claim file must stay confidential, plus the years it takes to migrate a large carrier and its vendors, exceed the time until that capability might exist. Mosca’s inequalityc states it plainly: if data must stay secret for x years and migration takes y years, you are exposed once quantum capability could arrive within x + y. For an insurer, x is measured in decades and y in years — the sum clears almost any horizon. And forward secrecy won’t save you: a captured session still holds an ephemeral key-exchange problem a future quantum solution can undo, and the metadata alone — who filed, when, claim amounts — carries value on its own.

What’s Actually Worth Harvesting

Not all data has the same half-life. A payment authorization loses value in minutes. A claim file—PII, VIN, damage photos, adjuster notes, and any attached medical records—stays identifying and exploitable for years. A Social Security number is effectively permanent. And a retention schedule is not a confidentiality period: it says how long you must keep the file, not how long its contents can hurt the policyholder—and an attacker’s copy survives your lawful deletion.

Crypto-Agility Is a Governance Problem

Swapping one algorithm for another is the easy half; the decisive half is whether you can find the vulnerable cryptography at all. Systems that label algorithm identifiers, key versions, retention periods, and data owners can locate what must move and prove it moved. A checklist that re-issues only public-facing certificates sails past code signing, database key-wrapping, backups, and the tunnels to repair networks, salvage vendors, and medical-bill review. Agility is observability and governance before it is a compiler flag.

Stop the Bleeding

Because you can’t un-leak a claim file, the most useful milestone is blunt: the date after which high-priority new data no longer relies solely on quantum-vulnerable key establishment. The standards are ready—in 2024 NIST finalized ML-KEM (FIPS 203),d ML-DSA (FIPS 204),e and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205).f And the obligations carriers already answer to point the same way: the GLBA Safeguards Rule,g the NAIC Insurance Data Security Model Law,h HIPAAi for the medical portions of a claim, and state breach-notification laws—none of which care when the attacker finally reads the data, only that you protected it for its promised life. Hybrid schemesj offer a controlled bridge while interoperability matures.

The Breach Outside Your Logs

The first large quantum computer will be a milestone, not a starting gun. For an insurer, the decisive event may already be behind us—a quiet copy of a claims archive, a stolen backup export—made years before anyone can read it, and impossible to recall. So the exercise isn’t defending against a 2032 machine; it is deciding, today, which of your claim files would still harm a policyholder then, and shrinking that set before it is collected: minimize what you retain, protect new exchanges with standardized post-quantum cryptography, re-protect stored archives, and build the agility to do it again. The one thing you will never get to do is un-file the claim.

Disclosure: AI tools were used for research assistance, reference gathering, and editorial support in preparing this post.

Footnotes

a. Shor’s algorithm. Wikipedia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shor%27s_algorithm

b. Grover’s algorithm. Wikipedia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover%27s_algorithm

c. Global Risk Institute. Quantum Threat Timeline Report (2021); https://globalriskinstitute.org/mp-files/quantum-threat-timeline-report-2021-full-report.pdf/

d. NIST FIPS 203, Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM); https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/203/final

e. NIST FIPS 204, Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA); https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/204/final

f. NIST FIPS 205, Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (SLH-DSA); https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/205/final

g. FTC. Safeguards Rule (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act); https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/rules/safeguards-rule

h. NAIC. Insurance Data Security Model Law (Model 668); https://content.naic.org/sites/default/files/modellaw-668.pdf

i. HHS, HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules; https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/laws-regulations/index.html

j. IETF RFC 9954. Hybrid Key Exchange in TLS 1.3; https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9954

k. NIST CSWP 39. Considerations for Achieving Crypto Agility; https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/cswp/39/upd1/considerations-for-achieving-crypto-agility/final

Sai Charan Obuladinne is a Staff Engineering Manager at GEICO, where he drives strategic technical initiatives for claims platforms in close collaboration with ML teams. Previously, he was a Staff Software Engineer at Meta, and he has spent over a decade building backend systems across advertising, healthcare, and logistics.

item.title: ‘We Are Not Ready for It’
item.dc:creator: Allyn Jackson
item.description: “Humanity needs everybody to think through this huge transition we are going through, because we are not ready for it.”
item.content:encoded:
Mathematicians the world over have been astonished by the rapid advances AI has made in their field. Many also are grieving the loss of the human-centered, hand-crafted spirit that characterized mathematics for centuries.

University of Toronto mathematician Jacob Tsimerman is grieving too, but he is not astonished. Over the past few years, even as he produced the work that earned him a Fields Medal in July 2026, he saw the AI onslaught coming. He also developed a deep conviction that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.

“AI and AI safety, I think, are the most important problems of our times,” said Tsimerman. He has shifted attention from his work in pure mathematics to focus on developing a theoretical basis for understanding and controlling AI. In September 2026, he founded the Mathematical AI Safety Institute (MAISI) together with Andrew Critch, a research scientist in the University of California Berkeley’s Center for Human-Compatible AI and chief executive officer of Encultured AI. Tsimerman serves as MAISI’s scientific director, Critch as its executive director.

Last summer, Tsimerman was planning to take a position in AI safety at OpenAI. However, after the establishment of MAISI, he decided to remain there full-time. OpenAI is supporting MAISI’s work in various ways, for example by donating credits and providing access to the latest models. MAISI is also cooperating with other labs and other AI safety organizations.

Starting with a $10-million grant from Coefficient Giving, MAISI is hiring between 10 and 30 theoreticians from various areas—including mathematics, physics, and computer science—for its January 2027 semester. Scores of further hires are planned. “What I want are people who are willing and able to work on hard problems for a long time and really tackle the underlying theoretical obstacles” to AI safety, said Tsimerman. “This is not going to be easy.”

Tsimerman’s career up to now has focused on purely mathematical questions at the intersection of number theory, model theory, and algebraic geometry. Nevertheless, he has been thinking seriously about AI for more than a decade. “I thought it was natural that, if AI becomes capable, it could become extraordinarily dangerous and risky,” he said. “But it wasn’t clear to me it would become capable.”

His doubts diminished when DeepMind developed the AlphaGo game-playing system in 2015, and disappeared when OpenAI released ChatGPT in 2022. “As soon as I saw that AI could talk, the debate was over for me,” said Tsimerman. “Now that it can talk, it can do everything.”

Critch and Tsimerman are co-authors of the paper “A Taxonomy of Omnicidal Futures Involving Artificial Intelligence.” When the paper was posted online in mid-2025, discussions of the existential threat of AI were on the periphery of public discourse. Today, they are center stage.

“Humanity needs not just mathematicians, it needs governance people, it needs infrastructure people, it needs physicists, computer scientists, chemists—it needs everybody to think through this huge transition we are going through,” said Tsimerman. “We need to figure out what to do, because we are not ready for it.”

CACM spoke with Tsimerman in early October. What follows is an edited version of the conversation.

What are your aspirations for MAISI?

My hope is to create some sort of theoretical underpinning for what safety is in some way that we can measure, for how to safely interact with an AI, for how to make the notion of AI alignment less fuzzy.

A good analogy to think about is the telecommunications industry. It was alive and well before we had a notion of what information was. Claude Shannon came along and defined—through entropy, which is a pretty math-y notion—how to measure information. That gave us a conceptual understanding that made the world leap forward. Now we measure everything in terms of bits and bandwidth, and we have Shannon capacity and measurements of how much information you can store.

So that would be a model of success. We want to come up with some version of AI safety that has a theoretical underpinning. Right now, we don’t have that. Right now, we do character training and monitoring. There’s a lot of hope in that, hope that the AI goes nicely forward, so maybe it will be nice in the future. I’m not saying that’s not worth doing; it’s definitely worth doing. But, as a place to hang the hat of civilizational safety, because those are the stakes, it’s wanting.

What you would consider to be progress in AI safety research?

I think there are several ways it could go. Any kind of metric to check whether alignment is taking place, something based more in fundamental understanding than on a sort of zoological treatment, would be useful. Any kind of protocol to deal with an AI that’s potentially untrustworthy but more computationally powerful than you, to allow you to trust the output even when you don’t trust the AI, that could be a success. Formal verification, formal methods, are something that people pursue now a lot with respect to AI safety.

I don’t equate safety with cybersecurity, because they’re not the same, and I think it’s quite damaging if we start thinking of them as the same. But cybersecurity and hacking are a big part of AI safety. Right now, the way a lot of cybersecurity works is we make software, and then we look for bugs. So we build a house and look for holes. That’s just not how you build a safe system. The AI can hack through that like butter. 

A better thing to do is to build something from the ground up that you can prove is secure, something that comes with a guarantee that information from a certain part can’t leak out to another part.

Is there an example of this idea being carried out, of building a secure system from the ground up?

Yes. For example, Kathleen Fisher, who is the CEO of ARIA [the U.K.’s Advanced Research & Invention Agency], ran a program at DARPA [the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency] called HACMS [High-Assurance Cyber-Military Systems]. It used formal methods to secure military vehicles. They gave a red team access, and asked, “How much could you hack this system?” And the answer was not at all, even with insider access. That demonstrated on a major scale—not nearly the scale we need, we need this to be everywhere—but on a major scale, that this is possible, within reach.

And it is more within reach with AI. A lot of stuff used to be out of scope because you just needed too much human time to code everything and make sure it’s okay. Now you can have AI write code and can formally check it to make sure that it’s correct. 

What areas of math will be useful and relevant in the work at MAISI?

I’ll answer your question, but first I want to emphasize the point that we want theoreticians. We are getting mathematicians, theoretical computer scientists, theoretical physicists, people who have done AI safety work before. We have a broad range.

Having said that, a lot of different parts of math could show up. When you’re interacting with a computational system and you’re coming up with some sort of interaction protocol or design mechanism, complexity theory shows up.

A lot of these problems are framed in terms of complexity theory problems, under which a lot of combinatorics takes place. We are doing learning theory, trying to understand how things evolve over time, how to understand the behavior of a large-scale system built of lots of neurons. 

A lot of statistical mechanics comes up, field theories show up, in which [partial differential equations] have a big part to play. Optimization and classical analysis have a big part to play. We are also trying to model AI by coming up with a game theory for AI systems that have to reflect on themselves and their internal structure. Logic and model theory also play a role.

The point is not so much to prove interesting theorems. I don’t really care if we prove a single theorem. The point is to develop some sort of understanding that we can then apply to AI safety.

What gives you hope at this moment in time, when things are changing so fast?

AI is becoming a part of our discourse, as it should. People are talking about the existential risks, they are discussing slowdowns and pauses, which I think is very good. A lot more energy and talent are coming forward. MAISI has had a tremendous amount of interest from theoreticians, which is not just good for MAISI but also shows that people are taking the problem of AI safety seriously. They are realizing the scale of the problem.

Humans are capable of great foolishness but also great wisdom. We have accomplished great things in the past, and we are still here. There are a lot of reasons for hope.

Allyn Jackson is a journalist specializing in mathematics and science and is based in German.

item.title: The Techlash Is Back
item.dc:creator: Moshe Y. Vardi
item.description: U.S. sentiment has turned negative on AI, with the majority concerned rather than optimistic about AI’s societal impact.
item.content:encoded:
Peggy Noonan is a weekly columnist for The Wall Street Journal. I often disagree with her opinions, but I find her to be one of the most astute observers of the American social-economical-political zeitgeist. When she described in 2018 Silicon Valley executives as “moral Martians who operate on some weird new postmodern ethical wavelength,” I realized that the popular view of Silicon Valley as a fountain of technical innovation and cool gadgets had changed. Indeed, in my January 2019 column,a I also quoted Niall Ferguson, a Hoover Institution historian, who described cyberspace as “cyberia, a dark and lawless realm where malevolent actors range.” The Economist magazine coined the term Techlash to describe what was then a new phenomenon of growing hostility toward the tech giants. The COVID pandemic distracted us from the techlash of the late 2010s. In fact, technology was our salvation during those dark days of social distancing. But now, the techlash is back!

In her Sept. 10, 2026 columnb “Pause AI for Humanity’s Sake,” Noonan argued, “When something speeds up and gets out of control, it isn’t alarmist to demand prudence and deliberation.” This is not the first call to slow down AI development. “Pause Giant AI Experiments: An Open Letter” was a letter published by the Future of Life Institute in March 2023. But The Wall Street Journal is, in essence, the flagship publication of the U.S. business community; the publication objects practically always to government regulation. A day earlier, Paul Tudor Jones, another columnist at The Wall Street Journal, warned that “AI May Become the Third Superpower”, and called for U.S. president Donald Trump and China president Xi Jingping to “develop a shared strategy to confront it.” As reported in the 2026 AI Index,c U.S. sentiment has turned negative on AI, with the majority concerned rather than optimistic about AI’s societal impact.

The negative view of AI has taken a concrete form in the backlash against datacenters, which emerged as a major factor in the November 2026 mid-term U.S. elections. A recent poll foundd that more than 70% of Americans oppose the constructions of datacenters in their areas because of “the strain on water and electricity resources but also the disruption to communities with noise and pollution.” The darkening view of AI technology and its impact is also translating into a darkening view of Big Tech. “Even the tech gods who once had good intentions have gone to the dark side, seduced by the billions to be made on [AI],” wrotee The New York Times columnist Maureen Dowd last February.

Last year, I arguedf that the pie-in-the-sky techno-optimism of some in the tech industry is bound to lead to adverse consequences. Bill Gates seems to agree with me; he recently warnedg that his industry was downplaying the risks, which he believes include mass unemployment and bioterrorism. Techno-optimism naturally leads to “techno-utopianism,”h which is the belief that new and speculative technologies are the primary drivers for human progress, societal transformation, and the extension of life

But in some segments of the tech industry, techno-utopianism has led to what is being called “Technofascism.”i If technology is an unalloyed good, then objections to it are simply bad and must be eliminated. Some techno-optimists are now advocating an authoritarian political model where unelected technology elites and corporate actors fuse private infrastructure with state power, using digital tools such as AI and ubiquitous surveillance to bypass and undermine democratic oversight. In a recent book, The Nerd Reich, journalist Gil Durán argues that a small circle of Silicon Valley billionaires and venture capitalists have concluded that democracy is in their way—and that they should be governing in its place. Undoubtedly, the technofascist view represents a very narrow segment in the Tech industry, but it is a very loud segment, and the rest of the industry does not object loudly.

Clearly, the time has come to boldly regulate AI. Beyond that, however, our professional associations still conduct their business as if academia and industry are two sides of the same coin. The Computing Research Association callsj for increasing interaction between industry and academia. Google provides financial support for the ACM A.M. Turing Award, fully funding the prestigious $1 million cash prize, in an apparent conflict of interest. If our professional associations are truly committed to the public good, then they must re-examine their relationship with the tech industry.
